headline: Process one breadth-first frontier at a time
statement: Return node values of a binary tree grouped by depth, from root level to deepest level. Within each level use left-to-right order. An empty tree produces an empty list. Trainer inputs use level-order arrays with null for absent children.
prerequisites: Basic Python lists, loops, and functions
intuition: Visit the tree one level at a time using a queue. At the start of a level, count the nodes already in the queue. Process exactly that many nodes, adding their children for the next level. This keeps children out of their parents' output group.
approach: Return [] for a missing root; otherwise enqueue it.
Pop size nodes, collect their values, and enqueue left then right children.
Append each finished level to levels.
correctness: Initially the queue contains exactly depth-zero nodes in left-to-right order. If that is true at one level, processing its frozen size enqueues only the next depth and preserves left-before-right parent order. Induction proves each collected group has exactly the intended depth and order.
bruteForce: Repeatedly scan the whole tree for each desired depth, taking O(n*h) time. A DFS with depth buckets is also linear but expresses the frontier less directly.

complexity.explanation: Each node is queued once; w is the largest level width. The queue during a level contains portions of two adjacent levels and remains O(w).

pitfalls: Freeze the level size before adding children.
Append left before right for left-to-right ordering.
Avoid list.pop(0), which shifts remaining entries.
